lead: Flight control systems carry a pilot's command to a moving surface, or carry it electronically to a computer and an actuator. This unit follows that path from a light aircraft's cables to an airliner's fly-by-wire computers, its autopilot and its engine control. After it you can trace any control chain, say why each stage exists, and size simple forces, tensions, loads and fuel flows.
about: Unit 1 follows one signal: the pilot's hands and feet, the machine that carries the command to a surface, and the loop that closes around it. Chapter 1.1 sets out why an aircraft needs controls at all and what a conventional chain contains. 1.2 compares the two mechanical carriers, rods and cables, and 1.3 shows why hydraulic power takes over on heavy, fast aircraft. 1.4 adds what a powered system loses, feel. 1.5 replaces the linkage with computers and wires, 1.6 closes the loop automatically with the autopilot, 1.7 pushes that loop into structural load control, and 1.8 applies the same digital-control thinking to the engine.

chapters.idea: An aircraft will not hold a wanted attitude or path by itself, so every aircraft needs a chain from cockpit control to aerodynamic surface: command, linkage, deflection, airload, motion.
chapters.depth: Cover the six degrees of freedom and the three axes with their primary surfaces: aileron for roll, elevator for pitch, rudder for yaw. Add secondary controls: flaps, slats, spoilers, trim tabs, and say what each does. List the parts of a conventional chain and the function of each: control column or stick, rudder pedals, throttle, bell crank, push-pull rod, cable, pulley, turnbuckle, quadrant, horn, hinge. Some syllabi call this the manual or mechanical control system. Use the Cessna 172R as the worked machine, a full mechanical single with a yoke, two pedals and a trim wheel. Stop at the parts; hinge-moment numbers come in 1.3.

figure.title: Conventional control chain
figure.aria: The pilot's demand passes through cockpit controls and mechanical linkage to a surface, whose airloads move the aircraft, and the pilot closes the loop by feel and sight.

chapters.example: The elevator of a light aircraft moves 25° when the control column travels 120 mm from neutral. (a) Find the gearing in mm of column travel per degree of elevator. (b) The pilot pulls with 60 N and the linkage gives a mechanical advantage of 4 from grip to elevator push rod; find the push-rod force. (c) The elevator horn arm is 80 mm; find the hinge moment the rod produces. Answer: (a) 120/25 = 4.8 mm per degree. (b) 60 × 4 = 240 N. (c) 240 × 0.08 = 19.2 N·m, which must beat the opposing aerodynamic hinge moment.
chapters.trap: Putting roll on the rudder. The rudder yaws the aircraft; the ailerons roll it and also cause adverse yaw. A second trap is saying a trim tab moves the aircraft: it moves the surface, and the surface moves the aircraft.
chapters.leave: Air data and engine instruments to Unit 3; display of attitude and modes to Unit 4; the navigation signals an autopilot couples to, to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: A mechanical system carries the command either with rods, which take push and pull and must be guided, or with cables, which take pull only and so always run in matched pairs.
chapters.depth: Push-pull rod: tube with end fittings and ball-jointed rod ends, bell cranks to redirect, idler levers and guides to stop sag and vibration, buckling limit on the compression stroke, backlash and thermal growth. Flexible push-pull cable (a conduit with an inner stranded core) for curved routes. Cable system: stranded steel cable, pulleys, fairleads, pressure seals through bulkheads, turnbuckles for pre-tension, tension regulators, rigging pins and rigging checks. Closed-loop pairs: one cable pulls while the other slackens. Compare friction, weight, backlash, wear, space, jamming and maintenance, and list the disadvantages of the mechanical system that lead to 1.3.

figure.title: Rod path and cable path
figure.aria: The stick motion splits at a bell crank into a rod path and a cable loop path, and both end at the surface horn that rotates the elevator.

chapters.example: A rudder cable is 3 m long, of cross-section 6 mm², steel with E = 200 GPa, and the turnbuckle pre-tensions it to 1.5 kN. (a) Find the stretch. (b) A push-pull rod of the same length with cross-section 50 mm² carries the same 1.5 kN in compression; find the stress. Answer: (a) ΔL = FL/(AE) = 1500 × 3/(6 × 10⁻⁶ × 200 × 10⁹) = 4500/(1.2 × 10⁶) = 3.75 × 10⁻³ m = 3.75 mm, which the rigging must absorb. (b) σ = F/A = 1500/(50 × 10⁻⁶) = 30 × 10⁶ Pa = 30 MPa, well inside steel's strength, so a rod fails by buckling, not by stress.
chapters.trap: Drawing one cable that both pushes and pulls the surface. A cable can only pull, so the surface needs a second cable pulling the other way.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1.1 for the parts and the surfaces they reach.
chapters.leave: Rigging schedules, inspection intervals and maintenance practice; structural buckling theory to the structures course.

chapters.idea: As size and speed grow, aerodynamic hinge moments outgrow a human arm, so hydraulics supplies the force: power-assisted systems keep the mechanical link and add a boost, fully powered systems delete the link and rely on actuators alone.
chapters.depth: Start from hinge moment M = qScC_h with q = ½ρV², S the surface area, c its chord and C_h the hinge moment coefficient, and show why M grows with the square of speed and the cube of size. Power-assisted (boost, servo-assisted, partial power): servo valve moved by the pilot, hydraulic actuator in parallel with the mechanical link, follow-up linkage that returns the valve, natural feel still present. Fully powered (all-powered, irreversible): no manual reversion, duplicated or triplicated hydraulic actuators, feel must be artificial. Power-actuated systems: electro-hydrostatic actuators, where an electric motor drives a local pump. Cover the challenges: single-point hydraulic failure, jammed surface, rate limiting, redundancy and dissimilarity, and why an irreversible system cannot be back-driven.

figure.title: Power-assisted loop
figure.aria: Pilot input opens a servo valve, hydraulic pressure drives the actuator, and a follow-up linkage returns the valve to neutral when the surface reaches the commanded position.

chapters.example: An elevator has area S = 4 m², chord c = 0.5 m and C_h = 0.15 at 100 m/s in air of density 1.225 kg/m³. (a) Find the hinge moment. (b) The pilot can give 200 N on a stick whose arm to the circuit is 0.30 m. Find the boost ratio needed. Answer: (a) q = ½ × 1.225 × 100² = 6125 Pa; M = qScC_h = 6125 × 4 × 0.5 × 0.15 = 1837.5 N·m. (b) pilot moment = 200 × 0.30 = 60 N·m; boost ratio = 1837.5/60 ≈ 30.6. At 200 m/s the same surface needs four times this moment, near 7350 N·m.
chapters.trap: Saying a fully powered aircraft needs no feel system. It is the exact opposite: with the link gone, an artificial feel system is the only thing giving the pilot any stick force.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1.2 for the mechanical link that the boost sits in parallel with.
chapters.leave: Hydraulic pumps, reservoirs, accumulators and typical circuit pressures to Unit 2; electric actuation power supply to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: An irreversible powered system gives the pilot no natural feel, so a Q-feel unit makes stick force rise with dynamic pressure q, and tabs do the same job aerodynamically by letting a small force move a large surface.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach Q-feel in this detail. Define q = ½ρV² and show why feel must follow it: a fixed spring makes the aircraft over-sensitive at high speed and heavy at low speed. The Q-feel chain: airspeed or q sensor, feel computer, bellows or capsule, spring gradient, plus a bob weight that adds stick force per g in a manoeuvre, and the trim release that moves the neutral point. Servo tab: a small tab geared to move opposite to the surface; its small hinge moment drives a large surface, so a manual aircraft can be flown by tab. Geared tab, spring tab, balance tab, and the anti-servo tab that moves with the surface to add feel and stability. Say which tab is a driving device and which is a feel device.

figure.aria: Stick force rises with the square of airspeed when feel follows dynamic pressure, while a plain spring gives the same force at every speed.

chapters.example: A Q-feel system is set to give 3 N of stick force per kilopascal of dynamic pressure, and the aircraft is trimmed at 75 m/s. Find the stick force needed to hold 150 m/s in air of density 1.225 kg/m³. Answer: q = ½ × 1.225 × 75² = 3445 Pa = 3.45 kPa, so force = 3 × 3.45 = 10.3 N. At 150 m/s, q = ½ × 1.225 × 150² = 13 781 Pa = 13.8 kPa, so force = 41.4 N. Doubling the speed quadruples the force, which is the point of the law.
chapters.trap: Mixing the servo tab with the anti-servo tab. The servo tab drives the surface; the anti-servo tab opposes the surface and adds feel, as on an all-moving tailplane.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1.3 for the irreversible powered system that has lost its natural feel.
chapters.leave: Trim switches, trim indicators and automatic trim as system hardware; stability and control derivatives to the aerodynamics course.

chapters.idea: Fly-by-wire replaces the mechanical link with wires and computers: pilot and sensor inputs go to redundant flight control computers whose control laws command the actuators, and fly-by-light replaces the wires with optical fibre.
chapters.depth: The chain: sidestick or column, rate gyros and accelerometers, air data, flight control computer with three or four lanes and voting, servo actuator (electro-hydrostatic or hydraulic), surface. Control laws: rate command, the C* law for pitch, normal, alternate and direct modes and what each gives up. Advantages: weight saved, no rigging, no friction or backlash, envelope protection and carefree handling, relaxed static stability made possible, gust alleviation. Disadvantages: dependence on electric power and computers, lightning and EMI, software validation. Digital FBW versus analog FBW, and its advantages: self-checking, gain scheduling by software, built-in-test, growth. Fly-by-light: optical fibre, the same chain, plus immunity to EMI and no ground loops, no spark hazard, low weight and high bandwidth, but bending radius, connector loss and optical power budget problems.

figure.title: Digital fly-by-wire chain
figure.aria: Pilot and air data inputs enter redundant flight control computers, which command an actuator, and the resulting motion is fed back through the inertial sensors.

chapters.example: A fly-by-wire computer has three independent lanes, each with a failure rate of 1 × 10⁻⁴ per flight hour. (a) Find the probability that all three lanes fail in one flight hour. (b) Repeat for a fourth lane. Answer: (a) lanes fail independently, so (1 × 10⁻⁴)³ = 1 × 10⁻¹² per hour, far below the 1 × 10⁻⁹ per hour usually demanded for a catastrophic failure. (b) (1 × 10⁻⁴)⁴ = 1 × 10⁻¹⁶ per hour. This is why voting lanes, not better single lanes, are the design answer.
chapters.trap: Saying fly-by-wire removes hydraulics or feel. It removes the mechanical linkage only; the actuators still need power and the pilot still needs artificial feel and a sidestick with a defined gradient.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 1.3 and 1.4 for powered actuation and artificial feel.
chapters.leave: ARINC 429, AFDX and fibre-optic data bus detail to Unit 4; DO-178B software levels to Unit 4; missile autopilots to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: An autopilot is the same control loop closed automatically: sensors measure the error between commanded and actual attitude or path, a computer shapes the correction, and servos move the surfaces or the throttles.
chapters.depth: Parts of the automatic flight control system: sensors (gyros, IMU, air data, radio altimeter), computer, servos, mode selector, disconnect. Inner loop holds attitude and rate; outer loop holds heading, altitude, speed or a navigation path. Why rate feedback damps: proportional alone overshoots, so the command is K_p × error − K_r × rate. Modes: pitch and roll hold, altitude hold, heading select, VOR/LOC/glide-slope coupling, autoland categories, low-speed and upset protection, and the disengagement logic. Auto-throttle (ATS): holds a speed or a thrust rating by moving the thrust levers, with modes such as speed hold, Mach hold and take-off/go-around, and its advantages in gusty air and on approach. Demonstrate on the Cessna 172R: a simple single-axis wing leveller with one servo on the ailerons and a turn coordinator as its sensor.

figure.aria: Automatic flight control splits into a fast inner attitude loop, a slower outer path loop, and the auto-throttle that sets thrust.

chapters.example: A roll channel uses 3° of aileron per degree of roll error and 0.8° of aileron per degree per second of roll rate, with rate subtracted. At one instant the aircraft is 4° left of the commanded bank and still rolling left at 2°/s. Find the aileron command and the share removed by rate feedback. Answer: δ = K_p e − K_r p = 3 × 4 − 0.8 × 2 = 12 − 1.6 = 10.4° of right aileron. The rate term takes away 1.6°, about 13 % of the proportional command, and that is what stops the overshoot.
chapters.trap: Saying the auto-throttle controls pitch or that the autopilot works without servos. The auto-throttle moves thrust levers only; on many light aircraft the autopilot is one axis and cannot hold height by itself.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 1.3 and 1.5 for the powered, computer-driven actuators the autopilot commands.
chapters.leave: Flight management systems and route programming to Unit 6; ILS and glide-slope signals to Unit 5; mode annunciation on the displays to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Active control technology uses the flight control surfaces for more than following the pilot: the computers also bend the aircraft's loads and stability, allowing a smaller tail, a lighter wing and a smoother ride.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this unit at this depth; some call it control configured vehicle. Cover relaxed static stability: the centre of gravity is pushed aft, the tail download and trim drag fall, fuel burn improves, but the aircraft cannot be flown without the computer. Then gust load alleviation and manoeuvre load alleviation, which sense acceleration and deflect surfaces to cut the peak bending moment; flutter suppression; ride smoothing; envelope limiting. Note the hardware: accelerometers and rate gyros, band-pass filters so the system ignores steady flight, and rate limits on the actuator. Note the certification argument: the function must be shown not to cause a worse load, and its failure must be shown to be safe. The saving is structural mass, because the wing is designed to the reduced load.

figure.aria: A gust pushes the wing to 2.5 g without active control, while gust load alleviation cuts the peak to 2.0 g and shortens the ringing.

chapters.example: A gust gives a peak limit load factor of 2.5 g. With gust load alleviation the peak falls to 2.0 g. The wing must be designed to 1.5 times the limit load. (a) Find both ultimate load factors. (b) Find the percentage reduction in design load. Answer: (a) without ACT, 1.5 × 2.5 = 3.75 g; with ACT, 1.5 × 2.0 = 3.0 g. (b) reduction = (3.75 − 3.0)/3.75 = 0.75/3.75 = 20 %, which is mass taken out of the wing structure.
chapters.trap: Saying active control makes an aircraft deliberately unstable for manoeuvrability. Relaxed static stability is the useful part, and it is only safe because the computer is there; losing it is a design case, not a nuisance.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1.5 for the fly-by-wire chain and 1.6 for closed-loop thinking.
chapters.leave: Flight management and route planning to Unit 6; actuator hydraulics to Unit 2; certification paperwork detail is outside this unit.

chapters.idea: The engine has its own control loop: from the throttle lever's demand it sets fuel flow and engine geometry to give the wanted thrust while keeping every limit, first with hydro-mechanical units and now with FADEC.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this as part of the control unit. Inputs: throttle lever angle, N1 and N2 spool speeds, EGT or TGT, fuel flow, inlet pressure P1 and temperature T1, oil pressure. Outputs: fuel metering valve, variable stator vanes, bleed valves, ignition, thrust reverser. Hydro-mechanical control: fuel control unit with a speed governor, acceleration enrichment, and limiters that stop over-temperature and surge. FADEC: electronic engine control with two channels, its own power supply, built-in test, ratings for take-off, maximum continuous and cruise, N1 as the thrust-setting parameter, EGT as the limit, auto-start, and data to the cockpit and to the auto-throttle. Say how the thrust lever asks for a rating and FADEC decides the fuel, and how it hands thrust demand to and from the automatic flight control system.

figure.title: Engine control loop
figure.aria: The lever sets a demand in the FADEC, which meters fuel to the engine, and the sensors return N1, N2 and EGT so the FADEC can correct the flow.

chapters.example: In cruise the FADEC meters fuel at 0.12 kg/s for 3 hours. (a) Find the fuel mass used. (b) Convert it to litres at a density of 0.8 kg/L. (c) Find the fuel cost at ₹90 per litre. Answer: (a) 0.12 × 3600 = 432 kg per hour, so 432 × 3 = 1296 kg. (b) 1296/0.8 = 1620 L. (c) 1620 × 90 = ₹1,45,800. The same numbers show why a 1 % improvement in specific fuel consumption matters to an airline.
chapters.trap: Saying FADEC moves the thrust lever. The lever is the pilot's demand; FADEC sets fuel flow and engine geometry. Also keep N1, the fan or low-pressure spool, apart from N2, the high-pressure spool: N1 usually sets thrust, EGT sets the limit.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1.6 for auto-throttle, and the closed-loop idea from chapters 1.3 and 1.5.
chapters.leave: Fuel and lubricating systems, ignition and starting to Unit 2; tachometer, EGT gauge and fuel quantity indication to Unit 3; engine data on the displays to Unit 4.
